edges.effect_quant: The strongest synthesis links antibiotic exposure during infancy to a modest increase in later asthma risk, with repeated courses and the earliest exposures looking more concerning than one-off later exposures. The signal is not huge, but it has been reproduced often enough to matter.
edges.population: children exposed to systemic antibiotics during infancy and followed into later childhood
edges.mechanism: Antibiotics can disrupt gut and airway microbial succession during a period when immune tolerance and Th1-Th2 balance are still forming. That microbiome perturbation, combined with confounding by infection severity, likely explains why the association looks modest but persistent in long-term follow-up.
edges.summary: Antibiotic exposure in the first year of life is associated with somewhat higher later asthma risk. The best observational literature suggests a small but recurring harmful signal, strongest with earlier and repeated exposure, making this more than a spurious one-study finding even though confounding cannot be eliminated.
edges.caveats: Respiratory infections themselves can predict later wheeze and asthma, so confounding by indication remains a major limitation. This edge should be read as a population-risk association, not as proof that every indicated infant antibiotic course causes asthma.

evidence.citation: ZhangZ et al 2021 World Allergy Organ J

effect_quant.comparator: infant antibiotic exposure versus no infant antibiotic exposure after addressing reverse causation and confounding by indication
